items.stem: In a Galton–Watson process, Zₙ denotes:
options: The population size in generation n
The offspring count of one individual
items.explanation: Zₙ is the number of individuals in generation n.

items.stem: The offspring PGF is:
items.explanation: The probability-generating function is the expectation of s raised to the offspring count.

items.stem: For a valid offspring PGF, f(1) equals:
items.explanation: Substituting one gives the sum of all offspring probabilities, which is one.

items.stem: The mean number of offspring is:
items.explanation: The derivative of the PGF at one equals the first factorial moment, which is the mean.

items.stem: Extinction by generation n means:
items.explanation: A family is extinct by generation n when that generation has no individuals.

items.stem: If K is Binomial(2,0.4), what is the mean offspring number?
items.explanation: The mean of Binomial(2,0.4) is 2×0.4=0.8.

items.stem: The extinction recursion for one founder is:
items.explanation: At generation zero the founder is present; the recursion follows by conditioning on offspring.

items.stem: The eventual extinction probability is:
options: The smallest root of f(s)=s in [0,1]
items.explanation: The extinction probability is the smallest fixed point in the unit interval.

items.stem: For a Binomial(2,p) offspring law, the PGF is:
items.explanation: The PGF of a binomial count is obtained by substituting s into its probability-generating polynomial.

items.stem: If m<1 in a non-degenerate Galton–Watson process, eventual extinction is:
items.explanation: A subcritical non-degenerate branching process becomes extinct almost surely.

items.stem: Which statements about the classical Galton–Watson model are true? A. Offspring counts are independent. B. They share one distribution. C. Zero offspring is possible in the model. D. The parent is counted in the next generation.
items.explanation: A, B and C are true; the next generation consists of offspring, not the parents.
statements: Offspring counts of different individuals are independent.
The offspring distribution is the same for all individuals and generations.
An individual may have zero offspring in the model.
The parent individual is counted as a member of the next generation.

A.why: Independence is a defining Galton–Watson assumption.

B.why: The classical model uses a common offspring distribution.

C.why: The probability p₀ may be positive.

D.why: The next generation contains offspring, not the parent.

items.stem: For f(s)=0.2+0.5s+0.3s², find the mean offspring number.
items.explanation: f′(s)=0.5+0.6s, so f′(1)=1.1. This follows by applying the offspring PGF definition and the stated generation rule.

items.stem: If Z₀=z and offspring mean is m, E[Zₙ] is:
items.explanation: The expected population multiplies by m in each generation.

items.stem: For f(s)=1/2+s²/2, starting from one founder, calculate q₁.
items.explanation: q₀=0 and q₁=f(0)=1/2. This follows by applying the offspring PGF definition and the stated generation rule.

items.stem: Which statements are correct? A. m=f′(1). B. q₀=0 for one founder. C. Eventual extinction q solves q=f(q). D. Any fixed point is automatically the extinction probability.
items.explanation: A, B and C are true; the smallest fixed point is selected, not any fixed point.
statements: The mean offspring number is f′(1).
The eventual extinction probability solves q=f(q).
Every fixed point in [0,1] is the extinction probability.

A.why: The derivative of the PGF at one gives the offspring mean.

B.why: The founder is alive at generation zero.

C.why: The eventual extinction probability is a fixed point.

D.why: The smallest fixed point is selected; another fixed point may exist.

items.stem: For Binomial(2,0.7) offspring, what is m?
items.explanation: m=2p=1.4. This follows by applying the offspring PGF definition and the stated generation rule.

items.stem: For Binomial(2,0.6) offspring, find the eventual extinction probability.
items.explanation: The roots are 1 and ((1−p)/p)²=(2/3)²=4/9; choose the smaller.

items.stem: If every individual has exactly one offspring with probability one, the extinction probability is:
items.explanation: The population remains at one individual in every generation, so extinction never occurs.

items.stem: For a supercritical Galton–Watson process with p₀>0, which statements are true? A. m>1. B. Extinction probability is below one. C. Survival probability is positive. D. Extinction is impossible.
items.explanation: A, B and C are true; extinction remains possible because p₀>0.
statements: Mean offspring is greater than one.
The extinction probability is strictly below one when p₀ is positive.
The probability of eventual survival is positive.
Extinction is impossible whenever the mean exceeds one.

A.why: The stem specifies a supercritical process, so m>1.

B.why: For a supercritical process with p₀>0, the smallest fixed point is below one.

C.why: A fixed-point extinction probability below one gives positive survival probability.

D.why: Extinction remains possible when p₀>0; it is not impossible.

items.stem: For offspring probabilities p₀=0.1, p₁=0.2, p₂=0.7, find the eventual extinction probability.
items.explanation: Solve 0.1+0.2q+0.7q²=q; the roots are 1 and 1/7.
